title: Fetch, JSON, and HTTP
runtime: Modern evergreen browser or Node.js with ES modules. Run fragments in browser DevTools or a small .js file unless the example says otherwise.

objectives.text: Create an HTTP request with fetch.
Check HTTP status before reading data.

Review after two and seven days

diagnostic.question: Can you explain the main purpose of fetch, json, and http before reading?
diagnostic.answer: A complete answer should name the problem it solves, the values or control flow involved, and one mistake to avoid.

sections.title: fetch starts a request
sections.body: fetch(url, options) returns a promise for a Response. The default method is GET. For JSON writes, set a method, a suitable Content-Type header, and JSON.stringify the body. The browser may also enforce origin and CORS rules before code can read a response.

sections.title: A response can be an HTTP failure
sections.body: fetch rejects for network-level failures, but a 404 or 500 normally fulfills with a Response. Check response.ok or response.status and throw a useful error when the application cannot continue. Then read the body once with json(), text(), or another matching method.

sections.title: JSON is a text format
sections.body: JSON.parse turns valid JSON text into JavaScript data, and JSON.stringify creates JSON text from supported data. JSON has objects, arrays, strings, numbers, booleans, and null, but no functions or undefined values. Parsing can throw, and successful parsing still does not prove the data has the shape your app expects.

sections.title: A request has UI states
sections.body: A useful interface represents the request lifecycle instead of assuming success. Start loading, clear or preserve earlier errors intentionally, handle non-OK responses, validate the received shape, show empty data separately from failure, and stop loading in finally. Abort obsolete requests when their result is no longer wanted.

sections.title: Why this matters in React
sections.body: Fetch, JSON, and HTTP is part of the JavaScript model React code already uses. Components, event handlers, state updates, list rendering, and data requests become easier to reason about when this concept is understood without framework shortcuts. Practise the JavaScript behavior first, then identify the same rule in JSX or a component.

interviewQuestions.followUp: Show a small example and one common mistake.

interviewQuestions.question: How would you prove that code using fetch, json, and http behaves correctly?
interviewQuestions.answer: State the expected value or control flow first, test normal and boundary cases, and inspect the actual runtime result. Explain the JavaScript rule behind the evidence.
interviewQuestions.followUp: Which edge case would you test first?

interviewQuestions.question: Where can fetch, json, and http affect React code?
interviewQuestions.answer: It can affect values, callbacks, rendering decisions, updates, or data flow. The exact connection depends on the concept; the important step is to reason from JavaScript behavior before blaming React.

commonMistakes.symptom: Code using fetch, json, and http produces a surprising value.
commonMistakes.cause: The result was run before the value, type, scope, identity, or control flow was predicted.
commonMistakes.fix: Reduce the case, write the expected result, and apply the exact rule from the matching section.

commonMistakes.symptom: A learner copies syntax but cannot adapt it.
commonMistakes.cause: The example was memorized without explaining why it works.
commonMistakes.fix: Change the data and names, predict again, and explain which behavior must stay the same.

commonMistakes.symptom: A React problem is blamed on React immediately.
commonMistakes.cause: The underlying JavaScript behavior was not isolated first.
commonMistakes.fix: Reproduce the value or function behavior in a small JavaScript example, then reconnect it to the component.
